articles.title: "It's like saving for a rainy day": perceptions of voice banking for people living with Motor Neurone Disease.
articles.abstract: This exploratory qualitative study examined how people living with Motor Neurone Disease (PlwMND) and their partners perceived voice banking and related voice preservation counseling within a specialist Australian service. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in 2022 with five PlwMND and two partners. Participants represented varying levels of engagement with voice banking, including individuals who had completed voice banking and those who had not commenced and therefore discussed voice banking conceptually. Participants described voice banking as a means of preserving identity and social connection, while also identifying uncertainty about timing, emotional readiness, and the practical demands of early action. Variable clinician knowledge, service navigation challenges, and confusion between voice preservation methods highlight the importance of informational counseling experiences. Findings are interpreted as reflections of participant perceptions at a specific point in time and within a single service context, rather than evaluations of current technological capability. The study highlights the importance of proactive, accurate, and staged informational counseling that reflects evolving voice preservation technologies and local service pathways.

articles.title: ABCD-Trial: study protocol for a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in patients with Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis for the evaluation of efficacy and safety of B-Cell Depletion with rituximab (ABCD).
articles.abstract: The exact disease-causing mechanisms in ALS remain incompletely understood. A possible cause is inflammation of neurons. Compared to other neurodegenerative diseases, neuroinflammation is pronounced in ALS, presumably leading to disease progression and neuronal death. Patients with ALS can have neuronal autoantibodies and most notably antibody-producing cells in the cerebrospinal fluid. The CD20-binding therapeutic antibody rituximab targets these antibody-producing B-cells. Rituximab is a medication commonly used in neurology. Single patients with ALS have already been treated with rituximab, which was well tolerated. We therefore want to evaluate safety and efficacy of a treatment with rituximab in ALS patients in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial. With this trial we aim for slower disease progression and unveiling disease-causing mechanisms in ALS. A total of 52 male and female patients older than 18 years with active sporadic ALS and disease duration of less than 24 months who are on a stable dose of riluzole (50 mg BID) should be included. Patients requiring assisted ventilation of any kind or have a known intolerance to the study medication rituximab are excluded. The study medication rituximab or placebo should be administered over a period of 52 weeks at 4 distinct time points, followed by a follow-up period of 79 weeks with 4 visits. Treatment efficacy should be evaluated using the ALS functioning scale ALSFRS-R-SE at every study visit (except safety visits). Safety will be assessed through regular laboratory analyses, adverse event (AE) and serious adverse event (SAE) monitoring, and CD20+ B-cell kinetics. The primary endpoint is the change in the ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R-SE) from baseline to week 79. Trial sites will be at Charité/DZNE Berlin and DZNE Bonn. ALS is a rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disease with limited treatment options. Recent preclinical in vivo studies suggest that B-cell-mediated autoimmunity contributes to disease progression. This trial will evaluate whether rituximab, which specifically depletes CD20+ B-cells, can slow ALS progression and provide insights into disease mechanisms. The trial was registered in the German WHO-recognized primary register Deutsches Register Klinische Studien DRKS (German Clinical Trials Register) on 3/07/2023 under registration number DRKS00030948.

articles.title: Cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and neurodegeneration biomarkers in the diagnosis and prognosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a multicohort observational study.
articles.abstract: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is an established biomarker for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, it remains unclear whether biomarkers reflecting amyloid-β metabolism (Aβ), tau (phosphorylated tau, pTau), and astrogliosis (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP) can complement NfL in clinical applications. It is also unclear how Alzheimer's disease (AD) co-pathology affects disease progression in ALS. We studied 264 patients with ALS and 164 disease-control participants, analysing baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) NfL, Aβ peptides, pTau181, pTau217, and GFAP. A two-step diagnostic strategy was examined in individuals with intermediate NfL values, using machine-learning models. Prognostic associations were evaluated using linear mixed-effects and Cox models adjusted for established predictors; survival was additionally examined in pooled analyses including an external ALS cohort (n = 153). Patients with ALS exhibited higher CSF NfL, Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, and pTau217 than controls, even within Aβ-negative subgroups. NfL discriminated ALS from controls with an AUC of 0.85 (0.82-0.88), which increased to 0.90 (0.88-0.92) in machine-learning models incorporating additional biomarkers. The machine-learning models maintained a high positive predictive value (0.90) for classifying cases with intermediate NfL values. Significant Aβ × NfL interactions were observed for longitudinal functional decline, and pooled survival analyses showed stronger associations between NfL and survival in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup (14%) than in the Aβ-negative ALS subgroup (HR 4.02 [2.17-7.45] vs 1.62 [1.36-1.92]). Multiple biomarker assessments can reduce misclassification of individuals with intermediate NfL values. CSF Aβ positivity modified the association between baseline NfL and disease progression. Personalised diagnosis and prognosis based on fine-grained co-pathology evaluation may enhance clinical management of ALS. This study was primarily supported by JST SPRING (JPMJSP2125). A complete list of funding organisations is provided in Acknowledgements.

articles.title: Factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: To identify demographic and clinical factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival using three well-characterized cohorts of patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). ALS patients from the Piemonte and Valle d'Aosta ALS Register (PARALS) diagnosed between 1995-2019 interval who underwent tracheostomy were included. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was used to identify factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival. Significant findings were tested in two independent cohorts, the Emilia-Romagna Region ALS Register (ERRALS) and an incident ALS cohort from South Sardinia. A total of 449 patients from PARALS underwent tracheostomy during the study period, with a median post-tracheostomy survival of 16.3 months (IQR 4.0-45.0). Younger age at tracheostomy was associated with longer survival (HR 1.03 per one-year increase, 95%CI1.01-1.05, p = 0.001), as being married/cohabiting (HR 0.78, 95%CI0.61-0.98, p = 0.033), a longer diagnosis-to-tracheostomy interval (HR 0.84 per one-year increase, 95%CI0.79-0.90, p < 0.001) and a lower ALS Functional Rating Scale slope from onset to tracheostomy (HR 1.13 per one-unit increase, 95%CI1.03-1.25, p = 0.012). These associations were replicated in the independent cohorts, when data were available. Additionally, discharge to nursing homes was associated with poorer survival in the Sardinian cohort (HR 4.23, 95%CI2.49-7.19; p < 0.001), whereas a more recent year of tracheostomy was associated with longer survival in the ERRALS cohort (HR 0.95, 95%CI0.90-0.99; p = 0.019). We identified multiple factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival in ALS patients, encompassing clinical and demographic characteristics at tracheostomy as well as local factors influencing peri- and post-operative care. These findings may support decision-making and clinician-patient communication in the advanced stages of ALS.

articles.title: The calibration-to-accuracy mapping in P300 spellers does not transport across cohorts and was not restored by tested alignment or local recalibration.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveA calibration-derived score has been related to online P300-speller accuracy in the same session, always within the cohort measured. We evaluated whether a mapping from that score to expected accuracy transports to withheld cohorts.ApproachRetrospective secondary analysis of BigP3BCI 1.0.0, the largest evaluation of this relationship to date: 18 of 20 studies contributed 271 participants, 739 session-condition records, and 19,611 character selections. The predictor was a decoder's cross-validated discriminability on calibration epochs, one study withheld from development. Between-cohort variation was summarised by the random-effects standard deviation tau.Main ResultsThe association was positive in all 18 cohorts but varied widely (r 0.190 to 0.928; participant-level r = 0.714, p < 0.001), with 12 CIs excluding zero. Pooled estimation error was 0.098 (95% CI 0.091 to 0.107) against a benchmark of 0.146. Calibration did not transport: intercept tau 0.87 (unrepresented-cohort interval -1.97 to 1.85, log-odds); cohort-specific slopes varied more than tenfold (tau 0.43, interval 0.111 to 2.005). Neither alignment (signal- or score-space) nor either nonlinear boundary meaningfully reduced this heterogeneity. Local recalibration with up to 16 participants did not reliably improve on transporting; refitting both intercept and slope was significantly worse than transporting at the smallest sizes. Median time per selection, a stopping-rule proxy, accounted for 66% of between-cohort slope variance in meta-regression. The four ALS cohorts gave an uncorrected slope spread of 0.223, against 0.560 overall.SignificanceThe evaluated score is a classifier's cross-validated discriminability on each session's calibration data rather than the source studies' undocumented online decoder. That score reproducibly signals within-session accuracy, but its mapping to accuracy is cohort-specific and supports ranking sessions after local validation rather than reporting accuracy elsewhere. The four-cohort ALS subgroup appeared more homogeneous than the full archive, illustrating how conclusions about transportability from a small cohort set can be fragile.&#xD.

articles.title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.
articles.abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.title: Mapping care interventions for people living with motor neurone disease: a living evidence and gap map.
articles.abstract: Motor neurone disease (MND) is a debilitating, life-limiting neurodegenerative disease that has no cure. Caring for a person living with MND requires a multidisciplinary team delivering interventions to address symptoms. We aimed to map evidence supporting care of those living with MND. Evidence and gap maps (EGMs) were developed according to Campbell and JBI guidance for scoping reviews. Databases searched included CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PsycINFO with no date restriction. Articles describing care interventions for people living with MND, carers, asymptomatic genetic carriers, family, friends, and healthcare professionals were included. 2390 reports were drawn from 1594 articles that were included across five EGMs, supportive and symptom management ( n = 673 articles), pharmacological ( n = 592), models of care ( n = 196), medical and clinical interventions ( n = 185), and technology and equipment ( n = 91). Interventions primarily addressed people who are living with MND ( n = 1732). No articles were identified specifically concerning First Nations Peoples, Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Peoples, or those living in remote, rural or regional areas. MND care interventions are diverse. Further research is needed to understand options for Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Peoples, First Nations Peoples, and those living in rural, regional, and remote communities.

articles.title: Protein disulphide isomerase protects against ALS/FTD phenotypes associated with cyclin F in zebrafish and cellular models.
articles.abstract: Mutations in CCNF , encoding cyclin F, cause a small proportion of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) cases. Mutant cyclin F mislocalises from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, impairs the ubiquitin proteasome system, disrupts endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to Golgi transport, and triggers ER stress and apoptosis. Protein disulphide isomerase (PDI), a redox-active ER chaperone of the thioredoxin superfamily, protects against ALS phenotypes induced by mutant SOD1, TDP-43, and FUS, but its activity against mutant cyclin F has not been examined. To test whether PDI overexpression prevents the cellular and behavioural phenotypes induced by the ALS/FTD-associated cyclin F S621G mutation. Neuro-2a cells were co-transfected with mCherry-tagged wild-type or mutant cyclin F S621G and V5-tagged PDI or empty vector. Subcellular localisation, XBP-1 and CHOP activation, proteasome reporter (GFPu) accumulation, nuclear morphology, and cleaved caspase-3 immunoreactivity were assessed by confocal microscopy. Transient transgenic zebrafish larvae generated by mRNA co-injection of cyclin F and PDI were assessed by photomotor response at 48 h post-fertilisation. Mutant cyclin F S621G induced cytoplasmic mislocalisation, ER stress (assessed by XBP-1 and CHOP activation), proteasome dysfunction (indicated by GFPu accumulation), and apoptosis (assessed by nuclear condensation and caspase-3 activation), all of which were significantly attenuated by PDI co-expression. Zebrafish larvae expressing cyclin F S621G swam significantly shorter distances than uninjected or wildtype controls, and co-expression of PDI restored motor function to near-wildtype levels. PDI protects against ALS/FTD-associated mutant cyclin F in both cellular and in vivo zebrafish models, identifying PDI as a redox-based therapeutic target for CCNF -linked ALS/FTD.
articles.journal: Redox report : communications in free radical research

articles.title: Cryo-EM advances in TDP-43 amyloid fibrils structure determination.
articles.abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a DNA/RNA-binding protein whose pathological aggregation characterizes a spectrum of neurodegenerative disorders known as TDP-43 proteinopathies, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Recent breakthroughs in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have revolutionized our understanding of these diseases by resolving the atomic structures of TDP-43 amyloid fibrils. These structural insights have been pivotal in elucidating the transition from functional liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to irreversible solid-state aggregation. This review synthesizes key cryo-EM findings from 2019 to 2026, encompassing fibrils formed by the full-length low-complexity domain, disease-relevant core fragments, and filaments extracted directly from patient tissues, as well as the pathological implications of distinct structural polymorphs. These findings not only deepen our understanding of the brain science aspects of the pathogenesis of TDP-43 proteinopathies, but also provide an important structural basis for the development of specific conformational diagnostic methods and targeted therapeutic drugs.

articles.title: Molecular recognition of axonal injury-associated candidate hub genes and predicted inhibitors across Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) have converging molecular pathologies such as neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and axonal degeneration, but do not have broadly effective disease-modifying therapies. A novel computational strategy was used in this study with an integrated in-silico pipeline to determine common candidate hub genes across AD, PD, and ALS and to computationally screen candidate inhibitors. The gene expression datasets were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus database and analyzed with limma R package for blood-derived gene expression datasets for AD (GSE63060), PD (GSE99039) and ALS (GSE112680). A multi-dataset intersection analysis revealed 138 genes commonly upregulated and 0 commonly downregulated genes, which were functionally enriched in immune regulation, apoptotic signaling and mitochondrial instability pathways. Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified three key genes (MMP9, PTPN6 and TNFRSF1A) as high-confidence candidate hub genes for AD, PD, and ALS. The ZINC library of 34,853 compounds was screened for drug-like properties using QikProp to yield 16,466 drug-like compounds. Based on the comparative screening results, the structure of MMP9 (PDB ID: 8K5Y) was chosen for further analysis and two of the selected compounds ZINC04582833, ZINC00047690 were identified as the two highest ranked compounds with docking scores of - 10.4 and - 9.7 kcal/mol respectively. Both complexes were further evaluated by 100 ns MD simulations, showing RMSD profile stability, maintained secondary structure for both complexes. The results in this study make ZINC04582833 and ZINC00047690 computationally prioritized candidates for shared neurodegenerative targets for experimental validation. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00774-6.

articles.title: Peripheral and cerebrospinal fluid inflammatory markers in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis an exploratory cross-sectional association study.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with an ambiguous etiology, whose onset may be linked to innate immune system activation outside the central nervous system (CNS). We investigated the association between peripheral blood and CNS inflammatory parameters in 45 sporadic ALS patients compared to 30 controls, analyzing peripheral blood tests (C-reactive protein [CRP], blood count, fibrinogen) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) immunological measures (Tumor Necrosis Factor alpha [TNF-α], TNF receptor type 1 [TNFR-1], CRP) alongside clinical characteristics. Results revealed significantly higher concentrations of TNFR-1 in the CSF of ALS patients compared to the control group (1,029.5 ± 176.0 vs. 846.1 ± 167.5 pg/ml; p < 0.0001). This difference remained significant in multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age and sex (OR 1.82 per 100 pg/ml increment, 95% CI 1.26-2.63; p = 0.0015). In an exploratory ROC analysis, CSF TNFR-1 discriminated patients from controls with an AUC of 0.78 (95% CI 0.67-0.88). TNFR-1 correlated with age (R = 0.32, p = 0.038), associations with disease severity and a lower concentration in bulbar-onset disease were exploratory and not robustly significant. Plasma and CSF CRP concentrations did not differ significantly between groups, but strongly correlated with each other in both ALS (R = 0.83) and control (R = 0.82) cohorts, indicating a disease-non-specific relationship. CSF TNFR-1 is independently associated with sporadic ALS and warrants further investigation as a candidate disease-associated inflammatory biomarker. Given the limitations, our findings do not prove diagnostic accuracy or causality. Longitudinal studies with disease controls and blood-CSF barrier integrity measures are needed.
articles.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

articles.title: Data-driven progression trajectories across clinical subtypes of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity; however, conventional classifications based on the predominant site of involvement may not fully capture patterns of disease progression. This study aimed to identify data-driven subtypes of ALS and reconstruct their temporal progression using item-level scores from the ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R). Baseline data from 3067 participants in the Pooled Resource Open-Access ALS Clinical Trials database were analyzed. Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) was applied to ALSFRS-R item scores to identify subtypes and infer their progression trajectories. Internal consistency was evaluated using complexity and sensitivity analyses. Longitudinal stability was assessed at 180 and 365 days. Associations with functional decline and survival were examined using adjusted statistical models. Three clinically interpretable subtypes were identified, characterized by predominant upper-limb, lower-limb, or bulbar involvement. These subtypes exhibited distinct, consistent progression patterns across the analyses. Subtype stability was moderate short-term but limited longer-term; stage progression was largely monotonic. The bulbar subtype showed more rapid functional decline at both 180 and 365 days. Higher SuStaIn stage was associated with increased mortality. In an exploratory stage-stratified analysis, poorer survival was observed in the bulbar subtype than in the upper-limb subtype within the lower-stage group. This study reconstructed ALS subtype-specific functional progression trajectories and inferred disease stage using a widely accessible clinical scale. SuStaIn-derived subtypes characterized patterns of functional heterogeneity, and higher stage was associated with increased mortality. Further prospective comparative validation is needed to establish the prognostic and clinical utility of this framework.
authors: Pooled Resource Open-Access ALS Clinical Trials Consortium

articles.title: Registry Forge: an open-source end-to-end pipeline for patient-directed SMART on FHIR registries.
articles.abstract: Patient-directed SMART on FHIR lets registries acquire longitudinal electronic health record data, but the payload requires substantial engineering before use. We present Registry Forge, an open-source pipeline that converts it into curation-ready outputs. Registry Forge parses C-CDA, HTML, RTF, PDF, and FHIR inputs, joins records to a canonical identifier, and emits a browser dashboard, an OMOP CDM v5.4 data set, GA4GH Phenopackets v2, a code inventory, and disease-specific narrative extractions. Applied to the ALS Research Collaborative Study (94 participants, 56 US health systems), it processed 22 686 files and 1791 FHIR Bundles (109 599 resources); only 15.0% of files were full C-CDA XML; HTML (48.4%) and RTF (34.3%) predominated. Payloads are far more heterogeneous than often assumed; the architecture is designed for extension, though generalizability remains to be demonstrated. Registry Forge closes the gap between acquisition and curation-ready data with no server infrastructure and is openly available.

articles.title: Salivary Dim-Light Melatonin Onset is Associated with Functional Decline, Respiratory Symptom Emergence, and Survival in Early Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Sleep-wake and circadian disturbances are increasingly recognized in people living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (plwALS), but endogenous circadian phase timing and its prognostic significance in early disease remain unclear. We assessed whether salivary dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO), an objective marker of central circadian phase, is altered in early plwALS and whether it provides prognostic information. In this prospective longitudinal observational study, plwALS within 18 months of symptom onset underwent home-based salivary melatonin sampling under dim-light conditions at 6 predefined time points around habitual sleep onset. Melatonin profiles were modeled using cubic smoothing splines, and DLMO was defined when the fitted curve first reached 3 pg/ml. Clinical, respiratory, and sleep assessments were collected at baseline (T0) and after 6 months (T6); a subgroup repeated saliva sampling at T6. Age- and sex-matched controls underwent melatonin profiling. Associations with disease progression, incident respiratory symptoms, and survival/tracheostomy were examined using regressions and survival analyses. A total of 50 plwALS were enrolled. Compared with controls, plwALS showed an earlier DLMO (20:24 ± 1:18 vs 20:58 ± 0:50; p = 0.028) despite similar habitual sleep onset and chronotype. Within ALS cohort, a later baseline DLMO correlated with worse functional/motor status, faster progression of disease, incident dyspnea/orthopnea by T6 (adjusted OR 3.11; p = 0.019), and poorer survival/tracheostomy-free outcome. In the resampled subgroup (n = 28), DLMO and melatonin-derived metrics did not change over ~6 months. Circadian phase alterations are detectable in early ALS. Baseline DLMO showed exploratory associations with functional, respiratory, and survival outcomes. Larger independent cohorts are required before DLMO can be considered a validated prognostic biomarker. ANN NEUROL 2026.

articles.title: An integrative transcriptomic atlas of ALS and aging skeletal muscle defines shared and distinct molecular programs of degeneration.
articles.abstract: Skeletal muscle atrophy and weakness resulting from loss of motor neuron innervation are shared hallmarks of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and age-associated sarcopenia. However, muscle wasting in ALS is rapid and severe, whereas sarcopenia progresses gradually over decades, peaking at an advanced age. The molecular mechanisms underlying muscle wasting in these conditions remain incompletely defined. Here, we used the SOD1 G93A ALS mouse model and wild-type mice across the lifespan to generate an integrated single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of skeletal muscle, mapping changes associated with ALS and aging. This atlas is complemented by structural and functional analyses. Our results identify transcriptionally distinct condition-specific myonuclear states, including disease-responsive programs within synaptic myonuclei at the neuromuscular junction, that are shared or distinct between the two conditions. Notably, at early stages, muscle from ALS mice exhibits molecular hallmarks of aged muscle at the myofiber level, indicating premature aging and reinforcing aging as a risk factor in ALS. At advanced disease stages and in old age, myonuclear subpopulations follow similar degenerative pathways in fast glycolytic fibers, consistent with their loss in both conditions. However, a distinct ALS-enriched myonuclei subpopulation displays uniquely regulated genes not observed in aged muscle, potentially underlying the more rapid and severe pathology observed in ALS. This atlas maps shared and divergent mechanisms of muscle degeneration in ALS and sarcopenia and provides a resource for identifying therapeutic targets tailored to each condition.
articles.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

articles.title: Ataxin-2 downregulation rewires neuronal and astrocytic metabolism to protect against TDP-43 toxicity.
articles.abstract: Ataxin-2 (ATXN2) is a genetic modifier of TDP-43 toxicity and a promising therapeutic target in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, the mechanisms underlying its neuroprotective effects remain poorly understood. Using global proteomic profiling in yeast and mouse TDP-43 models, we establish that pbp1/ataxin-2 (pbp1 is the yeast ataxin-2 ortholog) reduction confers neuroprotection by activating orthogonal stress-adaptive pathways in neurons and glia, rather than simply reversing TDP-43-induced damage. In neurons, ataxin-2 downregulation activates glycolysis and reductive glutamine carboxylation driven by IDH1, restoring ATP production independently of impaired mitochondria. In astrocytes, it upregulates cholesterol biosynthesis via HMGCS1, enhancing trophic support to neurons. Full neuroprotection requires both mechanisms: neuronal survival is only completely rescued when ataxin-2 is reduced in neuron-astrocyte co-cultures. Importantly, ataxin-2 downregulation protects against both TDP-43 gain- and loss-of-function toxicity, broadening its therapeutic relevance. Collectively, these findings establish ataxin-2 as a regulator of stress-adaptive metabolic resilience.

articles.title: Bullous Pemphigoid in Patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A Retrospective Study of 1,067 Cases.
articles.abstract: Background Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects motor neurons. Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is an autoimmune blistering disease associated with autoantibodies against BP180 and BP230. Previous studies have suggested an increased incidence of BP in patients with ALS. However, the neurological status and disease severity of patients with ALS at the time of BP onset remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to investigate the frequency and clinical characteristics of BP in patients with ALS.Methods In this retrospective study, we reviewed the medical records of 1,067 patients with ALS who were admitted to our institution between April 2010 and May 2025. Patients who developed BP after the onset of ALS were identified. BP was diagnosed by dermatologists based on clinical findings and, when available, by immunological or histopathological examinations. Disease severity at BP onset was assessed based on the ambulatory status and ventilatory support requirements.Results Seven of the 1,067 patients (0.66%) developed BP after ALS onset. The median interval between ALS and BP onset was 8.0 years (IQR 5.0-16.5). At BP onset, four patients (57.1%) were bedridden, four (57.1%) required tracheostomy and invasive ventilation, and two (28.6%) required non-invasive ventilation. Five patients (71.4%) required enteral feeding. The median age at BP onset was 68.0 years (IQR, 64.0-72.5). BP180 antibody testing was positive in three of the six patients. The lesions most commonly involved both the extremities and the trunk.Conclusion BP may occur more frequently in ALS patients than in the general population. Clinicians should consider BP when evaluating cutaneous lesions in patients with ALS.

articles.title: Corrigendum to "Exploring the cuproptosis-related molecular clusters in the peripheral blood of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis" [Comput. Biol. Med. 168, (2024), 107776].
Diagnostic evolution of carbonic anhydrase 3 (CA3) in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS): an emerging prognostic biomarker.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease traditionally viewed as a motor neuron disorder in which muscle atrophy occurs secondary to neuronal loss. However, recent clinical proteomic advances have highlighted carbonic anhydrase 3 (CA3), a muscle-enriched enzyme, as a promising biomarker associated with ALS disease progression. Therefore, considering ALS a neurocentric disease is not untenable. In this review, the authors examined the emergence of CA3 as an ALS biomarker and evaluated evidence from recent large-scale clinical consortium studies supporting its diagnostic and prognostic utility. They also compare CA3 with established biomarkers, neurofilament light chain (NEFL), a surrogate endpoint approved by the FDA. Discoveries of CA3 biomarker in ALS highlight that peripheral skeletal muscle is not merely a passive bystander, but an integral participant in ALS disease progression. Unlike NEFL, which primarily reflects neuroaxonal injury, CA3 may capture early neuromuscular dysfunction preceding motor neuron degeneration. CA3's emergence as an ALS biomarker supports a more integrated neuromuscular model of ALS and provides a compelling rationale for incorporating CA3 into multimodal diagnostic, prognostic, and pharmacodynamic biomarker panels to accelerate ALS drug discovery, therapeutic evaluation, and precision clinical trial development, highlighting their complementary roles in early diagnosis, patient stratification, and therapeutic clinical trial design.

articles.title: Interventions to support informal carers managing behavioral symptoms in frontotemporal lobar degeneration: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: Informal carers of people living with frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) face significant challenges in managing complex behavioral symptoms, yet disease specific support remains limited. This scoping review explored non-pharmacological interventions developed to support this carer population. Database searches were conducted across Medline, APA PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, E-Journals, and Scopus from January 2011 to November 2025, supplemented by hand searching, identifying nine included studies. Interventions broadly comprised occupational therapy-based activity programmes, psychoeducational approaches, and web-based self-management tools. The majority of studies were feasibility or acceptability studies, with findings generally positive; however, behavioral symptoms were inconsistently reported, and sample sizes were small, highlighting that evidence remains at an early stage. Despite the promising nature of existing approaches, structured implementation of non-pharmacological interventions to support informal carers manage behavioral symtoms into clinical practice remains absent. Translating feasible and acceptable interventions into accessible, disease-specific support for carers of people living with FTLD is urgently needed.

articles.title: Needs and Expectations of ALS Patients and Caregivers: An Integrated Perspective.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disease requiring complex multidisciplinary care. As disability advances, patients' and caregivers' needs may diverge. to assess needs, priorities and satisfaction with care among people with ALS (pALS) and their caregivers; to examine the association between satisfaction and Quality of life (QoL); to explore differences according to clinical characteristics; to understand the Italian ALS community's willingness to engage in research. In this cross-sectional multicentre study, 154 pALS and 211 caregivers were recruited (July 2021-November 2022). Structured interviews explored information received, care priorities, research expectations and satisfaction. Answers to the interview were compared between patients and caregivers and between different patients' subgroups with the chi-square or the Fisher's exact test. The scores of QoL questionnaires were compared between satisfied vs. unsatisfied with the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test in patients (ALSAQ-40) and caregivers (SF-36). Patients prioritized finding a cure (95%) and overcoming disease-related limitations (72%) over safe and tolerable drugs (55%), similarly to caregivers. Research on psychological and emotional support was rated more important by caregivers (70%) than patients (49%). QoL was higher among satisfied patients, with better ALSAQ-40 scores in mobility, daily activities, communication and emotional domains. Caregivers needing urgent psychological support were fewer among the satisfied (35%) than the not satisfied (50%), and SF-36 mental health scores were also higher in satisfied caregivers. Incorporating both pALS and caregiver perspectives into clinical practice and research planning may enhance patient- and family-centered care, improve QoL, and better align healthcare research and resources with societal needs.

articles.title: Protein arginine methylation rewires molecular interactions.
articles.abstract: Protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMT1-9) catalyze monomethylation and dimethylation of arginine residues in RNA- and DNA-associated proteins. Protein arginine methylation can weaken or strengthen nucleic acid binding, recruit or exclude protein partners, and promote or suppress higher-order assembly, making its molecular consequences highly context dependent. Methylation preserves the cationic character of the guanidinium group, while altering hydrogen-bond donor topology, steric accessibility, and interaction geometry. These effects are particularly consequential in intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), where arginine-rich motifs mediate multivalent protein-protein and protein-nucleic acid interactions. Here, we propose an interaction-equilibrium framework in which arginine methylation redistributes binding capacity among the competing protein, nucleic acid, and assembly states. This framework integrates reader-dependent and reader-independent effects of methylarginine and provides a chemical basis for understanding how a charge-preserving modification can reweight molecular interactions across diverse cellular contexts.

articles.title: Restoring Neural Homeostasis via Class II HDAC Modulation: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Opportunities.
articles.abstract: Class II histone deacetylases (HDACs) comprise class IIa enzymes HDAC4, HDAC5, HDAC7, and HDAC9 and class IIb enzymes HDAC6 and HDAC10, which differ substantially in structure, catalytic activity, subcellular localization, and neural function. Class IIa HDACs exhibit weak intrinsic deacetylase activity and function predominantly as signal-responsive scaffolds that couple calcium and kinase signaling to transcription through nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, recruitment of HDAC3-containing NCoR/SMRT corepressor complexes, and interactions with MEF2, CREB, and FOXO. Conversely, HDAC6 is a predominantly cytoplasmic deacetylase that regulates α-tubulin acetylation, cytoskeletal dynamics, axonal transport, autophagy, and proteostasis. Dysregulated class II HDAC signaling contributes to neurodegenerative diseases through convergent mechanisms involving synaptic dysfunction, maladaptive transcriptional repression, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and defective clearance of pathological proteins. Disease-associated substrates include amyloid-β and tau in Alzheimer's disease, α-synuclein in Parkinson's disease, mutant huntingtin in Huntington's disease, and TDP-43/SOD1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Emerging evidence additionally links aberrant HDAC4/5 signaling to neurodevelopmental disorders through altered synaptic maturation, excitation-inhibition balance, and circuit development. This review integrates the structural and mechanistic biology of class II HDACs with their disease-specific roles and evaluates therapeutic approaches to restore neural homeostasis. Particular emphasis is placed on selective HDAC6 inhibitors, modulation of class IIa protein-protein interactions and subcellular trafficking, natural compounds, and RNA-based strategies. Finally, we discuss major translational challenges, including isoform specificity, brain penetration, context-dependent functions, and the need to distinguish catalytic from non-enzymic mechanisms when developing disease-modifying interventions for neurological disorders while preserving normal essential HDAC functions and minimizing off-target toxicity.

articles.title: Mechanistic Evaluation of Psilocybin in Neurodegenerative Disorders: Relevance of 5-HT2A Receptors and Downstream Pathways.
articles.abstract: More than fifty million individuals worldwide are experiencing neurodegenerative disorders, which include Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, multiple sclerosis, and frontotemporal dementia. These disorders have a significant role in the gradual degradation of cognition and motor skills. Most current treatment approaches have little effect on changing the course of the disease and are largely symptomatic. Psilocybin, a naturally occurring tryptamine alkaloid from psilocybin mushrooms, has become a promising medicinal agent because of its hallucinogenic, neuroprotective, and neuroplastic properties. After being metabolically transformed into its active form, psilocin, it primarily activates serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. This modulates glutamatergic neurotransmission and neurotrophic signaling pathways such as BDNF/TrkB and mTOR, which regulate synaptic remodeling, dendritic complexity, neurogenesis, neuroinflammatory response, and default mode network connectivity, all of which are linked to depression and dementia. Preclinical research studies demonstrate that psilocybin increases hippocampal plasticity, restores dendritic complexity, lowers proinflammatory cytokine levels, and promotes fear extinction in experimental models of stress, ischemic stroke, and neurodegeneration. Emerging clinical studies also indicate that individuals with moderate cognitive impairment, early-onset Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease may see long-term decreases in anxiety and depression as well as improvements in cognitive function, frequently after a single dose administration. Additionally, psilocybin has demonstrated promise in treating mental comorbidities that often accompany neurodegenerative illness, such as treatment-resistant depression, drug use disorders, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. However, there are still significant obstacles to overcome, such as optimizing dosing schedules, assessing safety issues such as temporary perceptual abnormalities and cardiovascular consequences, and translating preclinical results into extensive phase -III clinical studies. This review incorporates the most recent data on psilocybin's chemistry, pharmacology, metabolism, and mechanistic actions; it highlights the drug's therapeutic potential across a variety of neurodegenerative diseases and emphasizes the necessity of carefully planned randomized controlled trials to determine clinical efficacy, long-term safety, and its place in multimodal treatment approaches.

articles.title: Progressive Supranuclear Palsy-Primary Lateral Sclerosis Overlap Syndrome in a Patient with a CYLD Variant.
articles.abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is an atypical parkinsonian syndrome characterized by progressive axial rigidity, vertical gaze palsy, dysarthria, and dysphagia. This report describes a case of PSP-primary lateral sclerosis overlap syndrome associated with a CYLD gene variant. We describe the case of a 59-year-old male patient who presented with slowing of movements and hypophonic speech. Neurological examination revealed hypomimia, dysarthric and hypophonic speech, restricted upward gaze, slow saccadic eye movements, rigidity and bradykinesia in all extremities, axial rigidity, brisk deep tendon reflexes, bilateral positive Hoffman's sign, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Brain MRI showed the "hummingbird sign" accompanied by bilateral cortico-spinal tract hyperintensity. MEP studies showed impaired excitability and conduction in the corticomotor system. Molecular genetic analysis identified a heterozygous G107A (c.320G>A; p.Gly107Asp) missense variant in the CYLD gene. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of PSP-Primary Lateral Sclerosis overlap syndrome was made. The contribution of the identified CYLD variant to this complex phenotype and its role in the neurodegenerative disease spectrum warrant further investigation.
articles.journal: Balkan journal of medical genetics : BJMG

articles.title: Revisiting the muscle spindle in ALS: Implications for spinal motor network dysfunction.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is typically characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons. However, the contribution of afferent sensory pathways to spinal motor network disorganization has received little attention. Converging human histological evidence from multiple independent laboratories demonstrates that fusimotor (gamma) motor neuron innervation of muscle spindles degenerates in ALS while sensory endings remain morphologically intact at the end organ, although the afferent neurons and ascending sensory pathways are also affected. This dissociation creates unmodulated proprioceptive input. Spindle-derived sensory signals reach spinal interneuron circuits without fusimotor gain-control adjustment, degrading spindles from forward sensory models encoding predicted kinematic states into crude stretch receptors. We propose that this gain-control failure, compounded by the loss of associated alpha-gamma coactivation and beta skeletofusimotor denervation, constitutes an upstream driver of the spinal inhibitory interneuron circuit dysfunction documented by recent electrophysiological studies in ALS. The resulting early disinhibition, followed by maladaptive excitation, mirrors cortical ALS pathophysiology. However, transgenic mouse ALS models show selective sparing of gamma motor neurons, unlike the human disease, constituting a critical translational limitation. We present a temporal model of human ALS, linking fusimotor denervation to progressive disruption of spinal inhibitory and excitatory circuits.
articles.journal: Pflugers Archiv : European journal of physiology

articles.title: Targeting protein misfolding and aggregation in neurodegenerative diseases: challenges for the identification and validation of targets for small molecules.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and related proteinopathies are characterized by the misfolding, aggregation, and accumulation of specific proteins that disrupt neuronal homeostasis, leading to neuronal death. Despite major advances in structural biology and molecular neuroscience, identifying and validating druggable targets in neurodegenerative diseases remains challenging. Many involved proteins are intrinsically disordered, exhibit conformational heterogeneity, and form highly dynamic toxic species. This review summarizes the mechanisms of protein folding, misfolding, aggregation, and prion-like propagation in major neurodegenerative proteinopathies, including amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD), alpha-synuclein (α-syn) in synucleinopathies, TDP-43 and FUS in ALS/FTLD, polyglutamine-expanded proteins, prion proteins, and rare hereditary amyloidosis. We also discuss major barriers to target identification and validation, including conformational flexibility, oligomer toxicity, blood-brain barrier penetration, and target engagement complexity. Finally, we highlight emerging strategies integrating structural biology, computational methods, and improved experimental models to discover small-molecule inhibitors for neurodegenerative diseases. Effective therapeutic discovery will require moving beyond single-target models toward ensemble-based validation strategies. Integrating structural biology, advanced imaging, biomarkers, and computational approaches may improve the identification of druggable targets and support precision-medicine-based interventions for neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.title: The small giant actor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases: Microtubules.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a clinically and pathologically diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuronal loss. Although research has traditionally focused on disease-associated protein misfolding and aggregation, increasing evidence implicates abnormalities of cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport in several neurodegenerative conditions. Microtubules contribute to neuronal polarity, axonal and dendritic transport, organelle distribution, and synaptic maintenance. These functions are regulated in part by tubulin isotypes, post-translational modifications collectively described as the tubulin code, microtubule-associated proteins, and molecular motors. This narrative review examines evidence linking alterations in these processes with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease. We summarize proposed interactions among microtubule instability, impaired axonal transport, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disease-associated proteins, including tau, α-synuclein, mutant huntingtin, TDP-43, and prion protein. Evidence connecting tau pathology with microtubule dysfunction is comparatively well established in Alzheimer's disease and MAPT-related tauopathies, whereas findings in other disorders are more heterogeneous and are frequently derived from cellular or animal models. We also discuss emerging experimental approaches, candidate biomarkers, and investigational microtubule-directed treatments. However, no tubulin-specific biomarker or microtubule-targeted disease-modifying treatment discussed in this review has yet been clinically validated. Overall, microtubule dysfunction may represent one component of broader, disease-specific pathological networks rather than a universal primary cause of neurodegeneration. Further longitudinal and clinical studies are needed to determine whether microtubule-related alterations act as causes, consequences, or modifiers of disease progression.

articles.title: Associations of self-reported and objectively measured physical activity and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis risk.
articles.journal: Journal of neurology, neurosurgery, and psychiatry

articles.title: Body composition characteristics in patients with inflammatory myopathy based on bioelectrical impedance analysis.
articles.abstract: To investigate body composition features in idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (IIM) using bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) and evaluate their clinical, diagnostic and follow-up value. This study included 103 patients with inflammatory myopathy over a 6-year period, excluding 15 cases, resulting in a final cohort of 88 IIM patients. Clinical assessments and BIA were performed. Healthy controls and patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) were independently recruited as separate comparison groups. IIM patients showed reduced muscle mass (SMM: 20.9±4.4 vs. 23.4±4.8, p=0.001), elevated ECW/TBW ratio (ECW/TBW total (ETT): 0.398±0.015 vs. 0.381±0.007, p<0.001), and decreased phase angle (PhARA: 3.50 [2.92, 4.50]° vs. 5.15 [4.50, 5.62]°, p<0.001; PhALA: 3.55 [2.84, 4.43]° vs. 5.03 [4.48, 5.42]°, p<0.001). These features correlated with disease severity, inflammation, and nutritional status. Compared to ALS, IIM patients had more marked ECW retention (ETT: 0.397±0.0145 vs. 0.389±0.0110, p=0.001) and impaired membrane integrity (PhARA: 3.450±0.99° vs. 4.295±1.44°, p=0.014; PhALA: 3.500 [2.850, 4.400]° vs. 4.400 [3.875, 4.925]°, p=0.003). Body composition demonstrated substantial potential for diagnostic application (XGBoost model: specificity 85.00%, sensitivity 88.46%), and more importantly, may serve as a valuable tool for disease management. BIA technology provides important novel disease characteristics for IIM patients, which are closely related to traditional clinical features and demonstrate significant diagnostic and management potential.

articles.title: Combined rituximab and magnesium acetyl taurate therapy attenuates neurodegeneration via ERK/c-JNK/P38MAPK signaling modulation in methylmercury-induced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like neurotoxicity.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor neuron degeneration, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and dysregulation of intracellular signaling pathways. The present study investigated the neuroprotective potential of rituximab (RTXMB), alone and in combination with magnesium acetyl taurate (MACT600), against methylmercury (MLMC5)-induced ALS-like pathology in adult Wistar rats through modulation of the ERK/c-JNK/P38MAPK signaling pathway. ALS was induced by oral administration of MLMC5 (5 mg/kg) for 21 days. RTXMB (50 and 100 mg/kg) and MACT600 (600 mg/kg) treatments were administered from day 22 to day 42. Behavioral assessments, neurochemical estimations, ELISA, Western blotting, hematological analysis, gross morphology, and histopathological evaluations were performed. MLMC5 exposure produced significant impairments in locomotion, muscular strength, cognition, and emotional behavior, accompanied by increased oxidative stress, inflammatory cytokines, glutamate excitotoxicity, apoptotic markers, methylmercury accumulation, and dysregulation of ERK/c-JNK/P38MAPK signaling. Moreover, MLMC5 caused marked demyelination, neuronal degeneration, neurotransmitter imbalance, skeletal muscle damage, and hematological dysfunction. RTXMB treatment significantly attenuated these pathological alterations in a dose-dependent manner, with RTXMB100 showing greater neuroprotective efficacy. Combined administration of RTXMB100 and MACT600 demonstrated the most pronounced therapeutic effects by restoring antioxidant defenses, suppressing neuroinflammation and apoptosis, normalizing neurotransmitter levels, preserving myelin integrity, and improving neuronal morphology. The findings suggest that RTXMB, particularly in combination with MACT600, exerts potent neuroprotective effects against ALS-like pathology via modulation of MAPK signaling pathways and may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for ALS management.

articles.title: Conformational allocation of mitofusin 2 in neuronal mitochondrial dynamics: Mechanisms and therapeutic targeting.
articles.abstract: Neurons must sustain functional mitochondria far from the cell body. Mitofusin 2 (MFN2), a dynamin-like large guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase), coordinates outer mitochondrial membrane remodeling with axonal transport, bioenergetic support, inter-organelle communication, and stress-responsive quality control. Studying these activities separately obscures how disruption of one protein produces diverse neuronal phenotypes. We propose a testable conformational-allocation framework in which molecular state distributions and transition kinetics bias MFN2 participation across cellular outputs. Integrating structural and functional evidence, we distinguish experimentally resolved mechanisms from working models. Variants associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A) are compared by the molecular step or functional output affected. Fusion loss alone does not capture this mechanistic diversity. Structure-guided docking supports local compatibility at a shallow, conformationally conditional C-terminal surface, without establishing native accessibility, affinity, or therapeutic response. CMT2A provides the strongest context for intervention, combining causal genetics, direct mitofusin engagement studies, and multiscale rescue. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) provides secondary preclinical evidence, whereas Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases remain exploratory. The mitofusin pathway is chemically tractable, but paralog selectivity and state-dependent target engagement remain unresolved. A state- and variant-informed strategy may better match intervention to the affected output than indiscriminate enhancement of fusion.

articles.title: Harnessing cGAS-STING in neurodegeneration: From mitochondrial DNA leakage and microglial reactivity to species-specific translational barriers.
articles.abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway, a cornerstone of innate immunity, has emerged as a critical driver of sterile neuroinflammation in the aging brain. Age-related decline in mitochondrial quality control, coupled with nuclear and lysosomal erosion, fosters the aberrant accumulation of cytosolic self-DNA, establishing a permissive environment for chronic cGAS-STING activation. This review synthesizes recent breakthroughs elucidating how major neurodegenerative diseases-Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease-converge on this pathway through distinct, disease-specific triggers, ranging from PINK1/Parkin deficiency-driven mitochondrial DNA leakage to TDP-43 proteinopathy-associated retrotransposon de-repression. Critically, we evaluate the translational landscape, highlighting the profound challenge posed by species-specific pharmacology, as exemplified by the failure of the covalent inhibitor H-151 to engage human STING. We argue that the future of therapeutic intervention lies not in wholesale pathway ablation, but in nuanced, context-dependent fine-tuning that disentangles its detrimental chronic effects from its indispensable homeostatic functions. This review positions the cGAS-STING axis as a promising yet delicate frontier for combating age-related neurodegeneration.

articles.title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

articles.title: Mapping the evidence on dignity therapy in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: Objective: To systematically map and synthesize the existing literature on the use of Dignity Therapy (DT) in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), with particular attention to feasibility, acceptability, therapeutic outcomes, and clinical adaptations required for patients and caregivers. Methods: A systematic scoping review was conducted searching PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Scopus for studies published in the last ten years examining DT in individuals with ALS. Eligible studies were charted and compared qualitatively due to heterogeneity in design, outcomes, and measurement tools. Results: A total of 237 records were identified, of which five met the eligibility criteria. DT was generally feasible in ALS, including in advanced disease stages, when adapted with augmentative communication devices, email correspondence, or videoconferencing. Acceptability was high across studies, with participants frequently reporting meaningful engagement with the narrative process and positive perceptions of the generativity document. Qualitative evidence indicated potential benefits in existential well-being, emotional adjustment, maintenance of identity, and family communication. Quantitative outcomes were inconsistent, showing variable effects on dignity-related distress, mood symptoms, and spiritual well-being. Caregiver responses were mixed, with some reporting perceived support and others noting limited immediate impact. Conclusions: DT appears to be a promising intervention for addressing existential and relational needs in ALS, though current evidence is limited by small sample sizes and methodological variability. Larger, methodologically rigorous studies are needed to clarify therapeutic effects, optimize delivery adaptations, and evaluate outcomes for both patients and caregivers.
